newsitem.title: USA: IMF sets date for multilateral Thailand loan talks.
newsitem.headline: IMF sets date for multilateral Thailand loan talks.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund set the date for talks about loans for Thailand on Thursday, bringing the biggest international lending programme since the 1995 Mexico crisis a step closer.

An IMF statement said lender states and international financial institutions would meet in Tokyo on Monday to discuss the multi-billion dollar package, designed to help tiger-economy Thailand recover from an economic mess.

"The IMF has convened a meeting of a number of interested countries and multilateral institutions in Tokyo on Monday August 11 to discuss their possible participation in a financing package for Thailand to support the stabilisation programme now being discussed," the statement said.
Late on Thursday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin issued a statement pledging U.S. support for an IMF support package for Thailand once a recovery programme was worked out.

Rubin said "encouraging reports" had been received from senior Treasury and Federal Reserve officials now in Bangkok for talks with Thai and IMF officials about the steps Thailand was taking to restore financial market stability and sustainable economic growth.

"Assuming conclusion of Thailand's technical discussions with the IMF on a strong and comprehensive recovery programme, the United States will fully support Thailand's extraordinary access to IMF resources," Rubin said.

Monetary sources in Washington declined to comment on the likely size of an aid package for Thailand, which sought IMF help reluctantly this week after weeks of procrastination following a currency crash.

Sources in the Thai finance ministry said earlier on Thursday that Thailand was likely to seek $7 billion from Japan, $4 billion from the IMF, $1 billion from the World Bank and $1 billion from the Asian Development Bank.

It would be the biggest funding package for a single country since the international financial community made almost $40 billion available to Mexico in 1995. Mexico did not use all the money and many of the loans have been repaid.

The IMF, seeking to avoid another Mexico-style crash, introduced new procedures to speed up loan approvals after the Mexico crisis. It used the new rules for the first time last month when it raced a $1.1 billion aid package for the Philippines through its bureaucratic cogs.
But Thai officials, jealous of their independence, wary of the IMF and keen to preserve their reputation as a booming "tiger economy", had initially been reluctant to ask for help.

A vulnerable currency and lack of investor confidence forced them to change their minds, especially after it became clear that bilateral aid would only be available as part of an IMF-supported package.

The assistance requested last week is being tied to the introduction of a tough austerity package, including a rise in value added tax, moves to cut the current account deficit and the suspension of more than half of Thai financial companies.
An international monetary source in Tokyo had said that the date of a meeting of potential lenders would depend on agreement being reached on the details of the IMF package.

"If the IMF and Thailand reach a final agreement there may be a meeting in Tokyo as early as next week to discuss the international financial support package for Thailand," the source said, speaking before the IMF statement was released.

He said the total package from Asian nations and international bodies was unlikely to exceed $15 billion, but he had no knowledge of the amount of financial support planned by private commercial banks.
Thailand has said it was seeking $12-$15 billion in loans from foreign countries and the IMF to stabilise its economy.
